title: Trump's Senior AI Policy Architect Is Leaving the White House
summary: Sriram Krishnan, the Trump administration's senior AI policy advisor, is stepping down at the end of June 2026. He plans to start an outside institution focused on AI policy, though its name and structure remain undisclosed. David Sacks, Krishnan's closest White House collaborator, indicated Krishnan would remain an outside adviser — an arrangement Krishnan has not independently confirmed in his own public statement.
body:
Sriram Krishnan will leave his role as senior White House AI policy advisor at the end of June, according to reporting first published by the Washington Post and confirmed within hours by Bloomberg, TechCrunch, The Hill, The Information, and Newsweek.

Krishnan came to the role from Andreessen Horowitz, where he had been a partner. His earlier career included senior positions at Microsoft, Twitter/X, Yahoo, Meta, and Snap.

Inside the administration, his fingerprints are on its most consequential AI policy moves. He contributed to the AI Action Plan, which prioritized data-center construction over regulatory frameworks. He worked on executive orders that pushed back on state-level AI regulations. He also helped shape oversight orders that were subsequently narrowed after industry objections — a pattern consistent with the administration's deference to the technology sector's preferences.

In a statement quoted across multiple outlets, Krishnan pointed to the unresolved problems he is carrying out of government: "Whether it is energy, data centers or a clear path for Americans to experience the benefits of AI, there are many tough issues we all need to navigate together."

He has announced plans to found an outside institution focused on those same issues. The institution's name and structure have not been publicly disclosed.

David Sacks, who TechCrunch identifies as the person Krishnan worked most closely with over the last 18 months, told the Washington Post that Krishnan intends to continue as an outside adviser to the White House. That arrangement comes from Sacks; Krishnan's own public statement does not confirm it. Sacks stepped down as AI and crypto czar earlier in 2026 and has since become co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST), which accounts for his continued White House advisory standing.

What Krishnan built over 18 months will not disappear with his government badge. The AI Action Plan, the data-center push, and the posture toward state-level regulation are in place. The question is whether his outside institution will carry real policy weight or serve primarily as a networking vehicle for a former official. That will depend on funding, structure, and staff — none of which are public yet.
ai_monologue: A White House AI architect who was a venture capitalist before he was a policy maker is leaving to build an institution that will try to shape AI policy from outside the government — the revolving door in reverse, or simply the same project with a different business card.

The two roles (former czar, current PCAST chair) explain why WaPo could plausibly describe him as having continued White House standing — he does, just in a different capacity.
